item.title: Isabelle Pool Server: a pooled verification service for prover training and multi-agent proving
item.description: Isabelle Pool Server (IPS), a verification service with a pool of warm headless Isabelle sessions behind an HTTP API, with session leasing and reclamation, memory-aware admission control, and a time budget on every call. Its verification interface spans single-step execution, block-level proof checking and whole-theory builds, with checkpoints for cheap branching and backtracking, and a build from scratch as the final arbiter. The service runs as a single container with monitoring and is accessible via a Python… — Xuanwei Ren, Wenda Li — arXiv cs.AI / cs.LG / cs.LO / cs.CL (AI for math)

item.title: Colombo: A Frontier-to-Frontier Autoresearch System for Oracle-Based Optimization
item.description: Science advances from frontier to frontier as discoveries reshape what is known and create the basis for further discovery. We present Colombo, a self-organizing AI researcher that drives this renewal, first instantiated in oracle-based optimization. Here, the central question is how efficiently a problem class can be solved through a prescribed information interface and what costs no admissible algorithm can avoid. The gap between achievable guarantees and unavoidable limits defines the frontier recorded in its… — Haihan Zhang, Wendao Wu, Chenheng Zhang, Chunyuan Zheng, Yanyi Li, Cong Fang — arXiv: lean

item.title: automodel: A Skill for Agentic Model Discovery
item.description: The search for better models, whether expressed as analytical equations or neural architectures, has increasingly shifted from manual design toward data-driven automation. While a multitude of algorithms exist, ranging from exhaustive search to AlphaEvolve, recent advances in general-purpose coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex raise the question: could providing such systems with a "model discovery recipe" be enough to discover or improve models? We present automodel, an agent skill for general… — Marco Virgolin, Harry Desmond, Ester Bergantin, Giorgio Morales, John W. Sheppard, Luigi Romano — arXiv cs.AI / cs.LG / cs.LO / cs.CL (AI for math) / arXiv gr-qc / astro-ph.CO / arXiv: ai discovery

item.title: Turing Agent: Agentic Formal Verification for Mathematical Research
item.description: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly advancing mathematical discovery, moving beyond benchmark-level problem solving to tackle frontier research problems. This progress is ushering mathematics into an era of proof abundance, raising a fundamental challenge: how can we ensure the correctness of the ever-growing volume of AI-generated proofs and transform them into trustworthy, machine-verified mathematical knowledge? We introduce Turing Agent, an agent harness designed to orchestrate end-to-end formal… — Yang Chen, Qianyi Wang, Ronghui Yang, Zhanhao Li, Yu Cong, Chen Zhang — arXiv: ai discovery

item.title: Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth
item.description: AlphaProof Code agents wrote three million lines of proofs in Lean to verify Signal’s core encryption. — Google DeepMind Blog

item.title: MCTS Is Counting the Wrong Thing: Learning Exploration Counts for LLM Reasoning
item.description: Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) has powered landmark successes in reinforcement learning, yet its gains in LLM reasoning can remain modest despite substantial search effort. We identify an overlooked bottleneck: what MCTS counts. Standard UCT assigns independent visit counts to textual branches, allowing different formulations of the same reasoning strategy to repeatedly receive exploration bonuses. Our theoretical analysis shows that this count fragmentation can impair exploration efficiency, as quantified by… — Xuan Zhang, Zhijian Zhou, Zicheng Hu, Yan Feng, Hongyan Hao, Yuan Qi — arXiv: llm math

item.title: Lean-Verified No-Go Theorems for $R$-Symmetries and Modular Symmetries in 4D GUTs
item.description: $R$-symmetries are instrumental in supersymmetric model building. However, a no-go theorem restricts us from using them in a large class of four-dimensional (4D) grand unified theories (GUTs). Specifically, it has been shown that a supersymmetric 4D GUT based on SU(5), with finitely many chiral multiplets, cannot be broken spontaneously to the exact minimal supersymmetric standard model (MSSM) while preserving a discrete $\mathbb{Z}_M^R$, with $M \geq 3$, or continuous U(1) $R$-symmetry. We use Lean 4 to… — Mu-Chun Chen, Xiang-Gan Liu, Michael Ratz, Alexander Stewart — arXiv: lean / arXiv: modularity

item.title: FunSearch and Structured SAT Search for Weak Schur Partitions
item.description: The weak Schur problem asks how large an interval of consecutive integers can be partitioned into a fixed number of classes with no class containing a monochromatic solution to $a+b=c$ with $a\neq b$. We investigate whether FunSearch, an evolutionary program-search method guided by a large language model, can discover effective construction strategies for this classical combinatorial problem. In our adaptation, FunSearch evolves a priority function used by a fixed greedy solver, while a separate validity check… — Rebecca Vicenzi, Pablo Christofferson, Caleb Hartman, Jingxuan Feng, Suleman Khan, Omar M. Elshinawy — arXiv: ai discovery

item.title: daVinci-Prover: Agent-Native Mid-Training for Formal Theorem Proving
item.description: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming formal theorem proving. Yet further progress remains constrained by the lack of a transparent and effective data recipe for systematically improving theorem-proving models. In this work, we argue that effective agentic provers require strong mathematical skill priors to ground theorem proving and agentic trajectories to enable long-horizon, interactive proof construction. To this end, we synthesize an agent-native 33.7B-token mid-training corpus… — Wenhong Zhu, Xuefeng Li, Jiashuo Zhang, Yu Chen, Tiantian Mi, Qipeng Guo — arXiv: lean

item.title: Statopia: A Prover--Library Ecosystem for Automated Formalization and Proof Discovery in Statistics
item.description: Theoretical results in statistics and machine learning rest on long, technically delicate proofs, and fluent arguments generated by large language models are not necessarily correct. Automated formalization makes such arguments mechanically checkable, and automated proving goes further by discovering machine-checked proofs for statements whose proofs are incomplete or missing altogether. Both require reconstructing assumptions from source materials, accessing specialized mathematical infrastructure and managing… — Ziyuan Chen, Tong Gan, Wei Zhang, Ruofei Fang, Boyue Tang, Zhenhua Lin — arXiv: lean

item.title: When Is Proof-Step Verification Worth Its Cost? Operating Requirements of Certify-or-Decline Verification for Open-Weight Mathematical Reasoning
item.description: Proof-step verification rewrites a solver's answer into typed steps and uses LLM judges to certify or decline. We evaluate this pipeline on open-weight models across GPQA, AIME-2025, and a MATH-500 subset. Certification raises answer-key-match precision by 31 percentage points on the strong GPQA configuration and 46 on AIME, while answering only 35% and 21% of attempts. On near-ceiling MATH-500, gains are at most 5 points at a loss of 13-27 points of coverage. An output-token-matched self-consistency selector… — Abhinav Gupta, Ben Slivinski, Yashica Patodia, Michael Saldivar — arXiv: llm math

item.description: Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth Google DeepMind — Google DeepMind / News: math-ai

item.title: LongTails: Automated Research in Optimization
item.description: We introduce LongTails, a framework for discovering and improving oracle-complexity bounds with formal verification in Lean 4. Using LongTails, we have already obtained more than 100 new results across a broad range of optimization problems, including generalized smoothness, heavy-tailed noise, finite-sum and composite optimization, and higher-order and zeroth-order methods. Our goal is to scale discovery and continually develop new methods with non-trivial and valuable theoretical guarantees using modern agentic… — Alexander Tyurin, QuocViet Pham, Valentin Khrulkov, Ivan Oseledets — arXiv: lean

item.title: Improving Analytic Constants via Interpretable AI-Guided Lean Proof Refinement
item.description: AI agents are increasingly capable of discovering new mathematical results, yet their reasoning and generated proofs can be difficult to understand and verify. We introduce an interpretable framework for AI-guided mathematical discovery, focused on improving quantitative bounds on analytic constants. Our key insight is that existing proofs often contain slack in intermediate lemmas, which can be tightened without reconstructing the entire argument. To exploit this structure, we represent proofs as… — Rahul Saha, Alan Li, Anton Xue, Swarat Chaudhuri, Adam Klivans, Pravesh K. Kothari — arXiv: ai discovery / arXiv: lean

item.title: TCSExam: Evaluating Frontier LLMs on the Full Range of TCS Research
item.description: Can large language models (LLMs) advance theoretical computer science and resolve its long-standing open conjectures? To study progress toward this goal, we introduce TCSExam, a unified framework and benchmark covering the full range of TCS research. It evaluates theorem proving, solver engineering, and constructions alongside direct attempts to resolve open conjectures, capturing both concrete research accomplishments and progress toward long-standing research goals. TCSExam-Full contains 100 expert-reviewed… — Yifan Luo, Zhengying Liu, Yang Yuan, Zhilin Yang, Andrew Chi-Chih Yao — arXiv: lean

item.title: Formal Proof of an Anisotropic Calderón Uniqueness Theorem
item.description: We announce a Lean~4 formal proof of a special case of the smooth anisotropic Calderón uniqueness theorem released by OpenAI on October 6, 2026. We consider smooth Riemannian metrics on the three-dimensional unit ball, with full boundary measurements and Euclidean extensions outside the ball. OpenAI's release did not include a Lean proof of their uniqueness result. Our formalization uses results from Mathlib and Tau Ceti, and it is given as a solution to a Lean comparator challenge whose check permits only the… — Cătălin I. Cârstea, Lauri Oksanen — arXiv: lean

item.title: Vertex Operator Algebras in Lean: a formal library and its companion book
item.description:
We present LeanVOA, a Lean 4 library for the theory of vertex operator algebras (VOAs), together with a companion book that sets each formalized result next to its textbook statement. The library constructs the Moonshine module $V^
atural$ and proves, with no hypotheses, the Conway-Norton moonshine conjecture for every automorphism of $V^
atural$ (Borcherds' theorem), along Borcherds' route through the Monster Lie algebra. It identifies $\mathrm{Aut}\,V^
atural$ with a formal model of the Monster taken from… — Fedor K. Popov, Leonardo Rastelli — arXiv: lean / arXiv: modularity / arXiv: tqft

item.title: LeanDojo-v2: A Comprehensive Library for AI-Assisted Theorem Proving in Lean
item.description: Building on recent progress in machine learning for formal theorem proving in Lean, we introduce LeanDojo-v2: an end-to-end framework that unifies repository data extraction, LLM fine-tuning, proof search, AI autocompletion, and LLM-assisted theorem proving in a single software library. In addition, we provide Lean4Code, a lightweight IDE that integrates the various features of LeanDojo-v2 through a simple, mathematician-friendly UI. These tools will enable mathematicians and researchers to easily fine-tune… — Ryan Hsiang, William Adkisson, Robert Joseph George, Anima Anandkumar — arXiv: lean

item.title: Lea: An Agent Backbone for Mathematician-Controlled Formalization in Lean
item.description: Agentic systems now formalize research-level mathematics in Lean, but they are built for autonomy: the mathematician states a target and inspects a result. The alternative, a general-purpose coding harness, is domain-neutral and must be assembled into a formalization workspace before any mathematics begins. Mathematicians, however, report wanting to keep high-level control over how an argument is decomposed and established. We present $\textbf{Lea}$, a Lean-specific agent backbone for mathematician-facing… — Shaswat Patel, Daniel Aarao Reis Arturi, Kevin Gomez, Jaume de Dios Pont, Jorge Poco, Eduardo V. Teixeira — arXiv: lean

item.title: Enhancing Mathematical Reasoning in Turkish Large Language Models with Search-Based Inference and Model Merging
item.description: We improve Turkish mathematical reasoning in Large Language Models by combining LoRA fine-tuning, weight-space model merging, and search-based inference. Using Turkish-Llama 8B-DPO with Turkish translations of MetaMath, NuminaMath, and TigerLab, we find data quality beats scale (Mix-30k best among fine-tuned; large MetaMath underperforms). Linear merging delivers the largest gains (GSM8K up to 0.63), while Ties is modest and Breadcrumbs/Slerp degrade. Search with MCTS and Tree of Thoughts improves mean LLM-judge… — Ahmed Zeer, Osama Shbib, Muzaffer Kaan Yuce, Himmet Toprak Kesgin, Mehmet Fatih Amasyali — arXiv: llm math

item.title: Autonomous AI Agents Systematically Diverge From Human Preferences in Proof Formalization
item.description: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems have ushered in a new age of proof abundance, but helping humans understand these proofs requires new attention to the differences in how AI agents and humans pursue a proof-making task. We present "simulated collaboration", a methodology that allows us to examine two key questions: (1) the relative attention AI agents pay to surface syntax or, conversely, deeper underlying semantics, and (2) how and where AI agent preferences for what to do next diverge from human… — Bálint Gyevnár, Simon DeDeo — arXiv: lean

item.title: zkARc: Succinctly Verifiable Proofs for Neurosymbolic Natural Language Formalization and Verification
item.description: Autonomous agents increasingly execute consequential actions on behalf of users, but ordinary middleware guardrails do not provide cryptographic proof that a policy was actually enforced. Their verdicts leave counterparties dependent on the operator unless they repeat the checks themselves, potentially exposing sensitive policies and inputs. We present zkARc, a modular proof-carrying framework that wraps each stage of Automated Reasoning checks (ARc) in an independent, succinctly verifiable zero-knowledge proof… — Wyatt Benno, Alberto Centelles, Aman Goel, Benjamin Kiesl-Reiter — arXiv: modularity

item.title: Lemmas and Conjectures in Spectral Graph Theory
item.description: The corpus of Elie Duhamel and Tristan Cazenave~\cite{dc} contains $305{,}755$ automatically generated conjectures relating spectral and metric invariants of connected graphs. A pipeline generated with Claude Code (numerical refutation, proof by the SMT solver \textsf{z3} from a library of lemmas, discovery of new lemmas, formalisation in \lean~4/Mathlib) refuted $162{,}964$ conjectures and proved $117{,}390$ without any unproved hypothesis, of which $79{,}505$ are verified end to end in \lean{} for every… — Tristan Cazenave — arXiv: lean

item.title: Math Foundation Formalization Agent: A General-Purpose Approach to Formalizing Mathematical Foundations
item.description: Mathematical formalization plays an important role in establishing rigorous and machine-verifiable foundations for mathematical reasoning. With the development of large language models (LLMs) and interactive theorem provers, intelligent agents offer a promising approach to automating the formalization of mathematical theories. This paper presents the Math Foundation Formalization Agent (MFF-Agent), a general-purpose intelligent agent designed to support formalization tasks across multiple mathematical domains… — Jiaxin Xie, Guowei Dou, Xiang Ji, Wensheng Yu — arXiv: autoformal / arXiv: llm math

item.title: Researcher-in-the-Loop Evolutionary Discovery of Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Code Families
item.description: LLM-guided program evolution can produce mathematical constructions, but validity, generality, and reproducibility require distinct evidence. We develop a researcher-in-the-loop discovery pipeline that combines program evolution, exact evaluation, mathematical generalization, certified nonexistence checks, and formal proof checking. We apply it to entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes (EAQECCs). Starting from tasks that did not specify a family formula, evolved programs produced finite qubit… — Jae-Hyun Baek, Byung-Sun Won, Jon-Lark Kim — arXiv: lean

item.title: A dataset of formalised theorem statements from the Annals of Mathematics
item.description: Recent progress in autoformalisation of mathematics using AI has been impressive. Measuring this progress requires datasets of formal statements that are both hard and trustworthy. We present AnnalsChallenge: 50 formalised theorem statements written by hand in Lean 4 using Mathlib. Each is the main result of a paper published in the Annals of Mathematics since 2020. Every formalisation was manually reviewed and then audited by AI. We release them without formalised proofs. — Thomas Browning, Katerina Hristova, David Ledvinka, Justus Springer, Hang Lu Su, Jack McKoen — arXiv: lean

item.title: DAPS: Dependency-Aware Premise Selection for LLM Theorem Proving
item.description: LLM-based theorem proving in Lean 4 has advanced rapidly, but provers are difficult to leverage newly contributed lemmas, because retrieval skews toward popular foundational lemmas, leaving the right premises buried among hundreds of thousands of candidates. Existing neural selectors rank candidates by semantic similarity, with three intrinsic limitations: frequency-skewed retrieval, isolated pairwise ranking, and degradation on out-of-distribution queries such as competition problems and informal language. Given… — Zixuan Chen, Wenyuan Jiang, Junling Wang, Mrinmaya Sachan, Yinya Huang — NeurIPS 2026 / arXiv: lean

item.title: Autoformalization for Ambiguous Inputs: Precision, Coverage, and Cost across SQL and Logical Forms
item.description: Agentic systems translate natural-language requests into executable artifacts while managing ambiguity and inference cost. We evaluate seven autoformalization workflows on SQL and first-order logic benchmarks for ambiguous inputs. Across five SQL workflows, the raw model leads with F1 of 53.35% on AMBROSIA and 60.85% on AmbiQT. On AmP, DRIFT gains 15.98 F1 points over the raw model at 2.03 times its token cost, whereas LoC uses 18.65 times the raw model's tokens with lower F1. Within AutoCedar, structured… — Henry Shen, Xinling Liao, Adarsh Vatsa, William Eiers — arXiv: autoformal

item.title: Scaling Lean Theorem Proving for Real-World Code Verification
item.description: We present EasyProver, a Lean proving system built from recursive agents with isolated contexts, asynchronous search, parallel tactic probing, and an elastic elaboration service. Using an off-the-shelf frontier model with no additional training, it proves 669/672 PutnamBench problems and all six IMO 2026 formalizations and resolves 597/600 NTP4VC verification conditions and all 189 VERINA tasks by proof or refutation. Because these benchmarks are close to saturation, we also introduce Aegis, which converts… — Debargha Ganguly, Divya Raghunathan, Dejan Jovanović, Vikash Singh, Soonho Kong, Aaron Tomb — arXiv: lean

item.title: Algebraic Completeness of Feynman Premeasures: The Henstock-Kurzweil Path Integral and Operator Wick Calculus in Lean 4
item.description: We formalize in Lean 4 the gauge closure of the Feynman functional integral for the free field without Wick rotation. First, the restriction to box divisions is removed via a direction bound and a uniform Riemann-sum estimate for all $δ$-fine cylindrical divisions. Second, the coordinate measure on $\mathbb{R}^k$ is identified with the standard Gaussian one. Third, the Saks-Henstock lemma and additivity are proved. Fourth, the Fresnel formula $\int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{i a x^2/2} dx = \sqrt{2π/a} e^{iπ/4}$ is proved… — Yu. N. Berdinsky — arXiv: lean

item.title: H$^2$R: Hierarchical Hint-Based Reward for Mathematical Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning
item.description: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards has shown great promise in enhancing mathematical reasoning in large language models. However, existing approaches provide limited intermediate supervision for complex, multi-step reasoning tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose \textbf{Hierarchical Hint-based Reward}, a framework that leverages the intrinsic sub-question structure of mathematical problems as structured intermediate conditioning signals during RLVR training. Unlike chain-of-thought prompting, these… — He Tu, Siye Li, Hongyi Wen — arXiv: llm math

item.title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
item.description: Papers in statistical theory rest on long proofs that few readers check line by line. We present KAPPA (Kit of Agents for Proof-checking Papers with a proof Assistant), open-source software that organizes language model agents, run by Claude Code, to translate the proofs of a LaTeX paper into the proof assistant Lean 4 with its library Mathlib and check them there, result by result. Each numbered result receives one of four verdicts: verified unconditionally; verified conditionally, with every cited or unproved… — Zihua She, Xiao Wang — arXiv: lean

item.title: MechAlign: Evaluating Semantic Alignment at the Project Level in Mathematical Formalization
item.description: Lean verifies that a formal proof establishes its stated proposition under declared assumptions, but does not check whether that proposition faithfully expresses the mathematical claim in a manuscript. Assessing this correspondence requires interpreting the main theorem through its project dependencies, which may be scattered throughout a large development. We introduce MechAlign, a framework for project-level semantic alignment review that combines formal dependency extraction with LLM-based assessment. Its… — Hao Shen, Ruichen Qiu, Lihong Zhi, Xiao-Shan Gao — arXiv: kakeya / arXiv: lean

item.title: h1: A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving
item.description: While progress in informal mathematics has come largely from scaling the chain-of-thought and agentic reasoning of frontier language models, formal theorem proving has increasingly relied on human-designed workflows around these models, such as planning, decomposition, and orchestrating specialized provers. This raises a bitter-lesson question: can a simple agentic loop that scales test-time compute match these workflows? The answer matters as formal verification must scale to keep up with frontier models… — Skander Moalla, Ahmad Rammal, Niket Patel, Remi Munos, Julia Kempe — arXiv: ai discovery / arXiv: autoformal / arXiv: lean

item.title: Connecting Quantum Proof Systems and Hoare Logic
item.description: Verifying quantum programs today requires specialized proof systems built on interactive theorem provers such as Rocq, Lean, Isabelle, or Why3, and even modest quantum algorithms cost substantial human effort to verify. Because quantum programs cannot be effectively checked by runtime testing, formal verification is the only viable path to correctness, making the cost of these bespoke systems the chief barrier to scalable quantum software assurance. We show that verifying a quantum program should be no harder… — Liyi Li, Zoukarneini Difaizi Tagba, Alex Potanin — arXiv: lean

item.title: Lean-QuantumAlg: A Framework for AI Agents to Produce Quantum Algorithms that Humans Can Trust
item.description: AI agents are increasingly capable of constructing quantum algorithms and proofs, yet machine-checked proofs alone cannot guarantee that the intended problem is solved or that resource claims match the verified computation. Here we introduce Lean-QuantumAlg, a Lean 4 framework for trustworthy AI-assisted development of quantum algorithms. Its Algorithm-Solves-Problem contract binds correctness, success probability, borrowed-state restoration and quantum and classical resource bounds to a single execution, while… — Lei Zhang, Mingrui Jing, Yusheng Zhao, Jiahong Liu, Xin Wang — arXiv: lean

item.title: Numina Fuse: Interactive Autoformalization in Lean 4
item.description: Numina Fuse is an agent-native application for formalizing mathematics in Lean 4. Since Lean can compile while not representing its intended informal meaning, and agents now write Lean faster than people can read it, we built Fuse around human supervision of agent work. A user works with an AI orchestrator on a Lean project and supervises it through views of the blueprint, the dependency graph, and the Lean code, while the backend keeps the project's derived state and runs agents for hours without the user… — Justin Asher, Yichuan Cao, Ruichen Qiu, Pietro Pellegrino, Jia Li — arXiv: autoformal / arXiv: kakeya / arXiv: lean

item.title: Self-similar solutions for the gSQG patch equations
item.description: The inviscid generalized surface quasi-geostrophic (gSQG) equations are a family of active scalar equations parametrized by a scalar $α$ that includes the two-dimensional Euler equations ($α= 0)$ and the SQG equation $(α= 1)$. We prove that, for every $α\in (\frac{7}{4}, 2)$ and every $T > 0$, there exists a self-similar patch solution whose boundary is a smooth, unbounded graph for $0 \leq t < T$ and develops a corner singularity at time $T$. The proof has been formally verified in Lean 4. — Javier Gómez-Serrano, Marcus Pasquariello — arXiv: lean

item.title: Formalising John Dee's Monas Hieroglyphica in Lean 4
item.description: John Dee's Monas Hieroglyphica (Antwerp, 1564) contains twenty-four numbered theorems about a single composite alchemical glyph, presented in the manner of Euclid: theorem, demonstration, corollary. In this note the following question is considered: which of Dee's theorems can be stated precisely in a proof assistant, and which of them can then be proved? Working in Lean 4 (v4.35.0) with the core library only (without Mathlib), we divide the treatise into three layers: the syntax of the glyph, encoded as… — Ivan Matychyn — arXiv: lean

item.title: Lean Finder V2: Semantic Search for Mathlib That Disambiguates User Queries
item.description: We introduce Lean Finder V2, a semantic search framework for Mathlib that disambiguates user queries through complementary model-level adversarial training and input-level query rewriting. Human mathematicians and coding agents rarely search Mathlib by providing detailed context. In practice, they query short properties, notation, aliases, or hypotheses, leaving much of the intended mathematics implicit. In contrast, existing Mathlib search engines unrealistically assume context-rich queries. The scarcity of… — Jialin Lu, Xiaoyu Liu, Hengrui Luo, Rodrigo Stehling, Linxi Liu, Weiran Sun — arXiv: lean

item.title: PaperFormalizer: Author-in-the-Loop Autoformalization of Research Papers in Lean
item.description: Even a carefully proofread paper can leave small gaps in its proofs or its stated assumptions. We introduce PaperFormalizer, a Lean-based agentic pipeline that helps authors find and close such gaps in their own papers and turn each paper into a Lean-verified version. Starting from the LaTeX source, PaperFormalizer transcribes the paper into a dependency graph of statements, audits each statement in natural language for faithfulness, ambiguity and correctness, and then formalizes and proves the statements in Lean… — Jiyuan Tan, Jose Blanchet, Vasilis Syrgkanis — arXiv: autoformal / arXiv: lean

item.title: The irrationality exponent of the lemniscate period: A determinant proof with a Lean 4 formalization
item.description: Let $Ω=2\int_0^1(1-t^4)^{-1/2}dt$. We prove that, for every real $ν>2$, there is $Q\geq2$ such that $q^{-ν}<|Ω-p/q|$ for every integer $p$ and every integer $q\geq Q$. Consequently $Ω$ is irrational and its irrationality exponent is two. The proof combines elliptic separated-weight interpolation, arithmetic denominator estimates, and an analytic determinant bound on a square complex-multiplication grid. The determinant comparison uses the same selected source columns on both sides. We give the integral-to-lattice… — Gregory V. Chudnovsky — arXiv: lean

item.title: ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
item.description: Evolutionary coding agents such as AlphaEvolve are one of the notable successes in using Large Language Models (LLMs) to build AI Scientists. These agents tackle open-ended scientific problems by iteratively improving and evolving programs, leveraging the prior knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Despite their success, mutations over programs are mostly low-level upon surface heuristics, without a persistent unit of control. In contrast, science compounds through ideas. In this work, we propose… — Yongqiang Chen, Chenxi Liu, Deyu Zou, Zhenhao Chen, Tongliang Liu, Bo Han — arXiv: ai discovery

item.title: Maestro: Agentic Formal Proof Development by Coordination
item.description: Lean is increasingly used to verify mathematical proofs and software produced by LLM agents, but writing formal proofs remains hard. Existing prover systems take a divide-and-conquer approach that recursively decomposes hard proof goals into easier lemmas and splits again any lemma that resists proof. However, a lemma can resist proof for different reasons, including insufficient guidance, a false statement, or a flaw in the decomposition that produced it. Existing systems cannot tell these apart as a failed… — Haoyu Li, Zeren Shui, Yuhao Zhang, Ferhat Erata, Benjamin Mikek, Murali Krishna Ramanathan — arXiv: lean

item.title: ReuF2F: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Formalized Undergraduate Research Problems
item.description: As AI systems begin to resolve open research problems, reliable verification becomes increasingly important. Formal mathematics provides a trusted framework for mathematical reasoning, enabling agents to produce machine-checkable proofs while conducting mathematical exploration. Existing formal mathematics benchmarks often focus on known results or a small set of prominent open problems, which can become difficult to evaluate reliably once solutions are discovered and widely disseminated. Existing evaluation… — Zeyu Zheng, Yiyang Liu, Yuyang Zhao, Congmin Zheng, Jiachen Zhu, Jianian Chen — arXiv: autoformal / arXiv: lean

item.title: Attention-Graph Curvature for the Verification of Mathematical Reasoning
item.description: Language models have recently solved open Erdős problems and achieved gold-medal level performance on International Mathematical Olympiad problems. But their solutions, written in natural language, cannot yet be verified by proof assistants. An erroneous reasoning step can invalidate every step that comes after, so it is advantageous to detect errors early. Several methods have been proposed to detect erroneous reasoning quickly based on the features of the forward pass of the language model that performs… — Kanghyeon Kim, Johannes F. Lutzeyer, Yanzhu Guo — arXiv: llm math

item.title: Smale's sixth problem for five bodies in the plane, with a proof formalized in Lean
item.description: We prove that for every choice of five positive masses the planar five-body problem has finitely many central configurations up to similarity. This settles Smale's sixth problem for five bodies in the plane. Albouy and Kaloshin proved it for masses outside a closed algebraic subset of codimension two. We follow their method. Infinitely many central configurations would give an algebraic curve of complex solutions. At the places at infinity of the curve the valuations of the mutual distances must balance. We… — Tejasvi Singh Tomar — arXiv: lean

item.title: Euler: Towards Human-Centered Multi-Agent Mathematical Discovery
item.description: Mathematical research drives scientific discovery, and recent advances in AI for mathematics have shown that language-model agents can solve challenging problems and develop substantial mathematical proofs. Yet much of today's AI-for-mathematics work centers on obtaining a final answer. This emphasis leaves the exploration behind a result difficult for researchers to understand, while long-running investigations face fragmented context and the risk of unsupported claims propagating across reasoning steps. We… — Qiuyu Chen, Qi Wang, Liang Xu, Xin Jin, Baao Xie, Wenjun Zeng — arXiv: ai discovery

item.title: MAMath-Bench: Process-Aware and Robust Evaluation of Multimodal Multi-Agent Mathematical Reasoning
item.description: Mathematical reasoning is a fundamental capability for educational applications of Large Language Models (LLMs), where reliable problem solving requires not only correct answers but also coherent and verifiable reasoning processes. Multi-agent systems (MASs) have shown growing potential in this domain by leveraging collaboration and verification among multiple LLM agents. However, existing evaluations primarily focus on the correctness of final answers in text-only settings, offering limited insight into… — Xinping Wang, Jie Ma, Rui Xing, Wensong Guo, Xiayi Zhang, Jianhao Deng — arXiv: llm math

item.title: Repair, Retry, and the Cost of Hindsight: Verifier Feedback in Formal Theorem Proving
item.description: Verifier-guided self-repair conditions a model on feedback from failed attempts before it tries again, without weight updates. Yet two findings in prior work are in tension: verifier feedback can improve repair of failures, but self-repair itself can provide little-to-no advantage over independent resampling. item.title: Proof Perplexity: A Probabilistic Approach to Measuring non-triviality in Machine Generated Proofs
item.description: In this article, we propose a benchmark to quantify the non-triviality and novelty of machine-generated mathematical proofs compared to existing literature. Our core methodology uses a probabilistic measure to evaluate the non-triviality of the underlying mathematical arguments in comparison to the current \texttt{MATHLIB} library. Finally, we apply this benchmark to the recent proof generated by Claude on the complex zeros of the Riemann zeta function to test for non-trivial steps. — Madhuparna Das, Soumya Banerjee — arXiv: riemann

item.title: Lean Graph Search for Formal Theorem Proving
item.description: Retrieving relevant lemmas is crucial for formal theorem proving, enabling provers to build machine-checkable proofs from established mathematical results. Recent retrieval systems match library declarations to a target theorem or its intermediate proof steps, but make limited use of multi-hop dependencies among declarations. These dependencies can reveal supporting lemmas that are not necessarily lexically similar to the target theorem but recur in proofs of related problems. item.title: A Lean Formalization of the Hamilton--Perelman Proof of Thurston's Geometrization Conjecture
item.description: We formalize the Hamilton--Perelman Ricci-flow proof of Thurston's geometrization conjecture. The public Lean declaration is reproduced in this paper. item.title: An AI-Assisted Formalization of the Poincaré Conjecture
item.description: We present an AI-assisted Lean 4 formalization of the Poincaré conjecture. The project began with limited reusable formal infrastructure for the geometric analysis behind the proof. To organize this work, we combined a proof blueprint prepared by mathematicians with explicit milestone statements. item.title: Beyond LLM Judge: Mechanical Verification for Agentic Autoformalization
item.description: We introduce a novel method for verifying Lean formalizations that goes beyond LLM-judged faithfulness. Unlike most verification methods, which rely on LLMs or trained models, our method combines LLM-based semantic review with mechanical numerical and vacuity checks, providing checkable feedback and detecting errors missed by LLM judges. item.title: Quantum Cryptography and Autoformalization in Lean
item.description: Quantum key distribution provides secure communication by relying on physics principles and mathematical reasoning. Security proofs across the field can contain gaps, often between individually valid theorems integrated under mismatched assumptions. We produce an end-to-end security theorem formalized in the Lean proof assistant, eliminating hidden hypotheses by building only on Lean's standard axioms. item.title: Aligning Information Theory and Formal Verification: A Lean Formalization of Rate-Distortion Theory
item.description: Large language models have recently demonstrated an ability to generate substantial mathematical proofs and formalizations, including machine-checked arguments for major open problems and classical theorems. These developments highlight a growing workflow in which AI systems search for proofs while proof assistants certify their correctness. item.title: Do Theorem Provers Need Theorem-Proving Agents? mini-Lean-agent: A Coding-Agent Baseline for Lean
item.description: General-purpose coding agents use standard shell and file interactions, yet formal theorem-proving agents often rely on specialized, ad-hoc tooling. This makes it difficult to determine which components of theorem-proving agents provide benchmark gains: an improved base model, a specialized harness, a specific tool, or a combination of any of them. item.title: Masked Attention Pooling Is Invariant to Padding and Permutation: A Formal Proof in Lean
item.description: Attention-based multiple instance learning (MIL) pools a variable-size bag of instance embeddings into one vector. In batched training, bags are padded to a common length, and the pooled output is expected not to depend on how much padding was added or on the order in which instances are stored. item.title: The Bloch constant is strictly smaller than the Ahlfors--Grunsky value
item.description: We prove that the classical Bloch constant is strictly smaller than the Ahlfors--Grunsky value, disproving the famous Bloch constant conjecture. The Lean 4 formalization of the main results are also provided. — Teng Zhang — arXiv: lean

item.title: Definition Grounding in Theory-Level Auto-formalization
item.description: LLM-based auto-formalization systems can now generate formally verified Lean code at unprecedented rates. However, a formalization advances mathematical research only when further mathematical results can be built on it, especially when its definitions and helper lemmas are general enough to be imported and used idiomatically. We propose definition grounding, where definition formalizations are continuously judged and revised, as a method to ensure formalization quality. item.title: Aligning Faithfulness for Theory-Scale Autoformalization
item.description: Autoformalization (AF) requires more than compilation: formal statements must preserve the meaning of their informal sources, a property known as faithfulness. An emerging frontier is the automated evaluation of this property, yet most existing methods operate at the statement level and produce whole-item verdicts, failing to reveal how individual expressions correspond or which contextual interpretations support the judgment. This omission is consequential because AF is inherently theory-scale: target statements… — Yuming Feng, Tadd Mao, Dhruva Arekar, Tianjun Zhong, Jiani Huang, Xujie Si — arXiv: autoformal

item.title: Continual Graph Memory and Community Infrastructure for AI-Assisted Mathematical Discovery
item.description: Mathematical discovery requires preserving partial ideas and the evidence supporting their reuse. We present Ansatz, a research harness whose continual graph memory separates model-accepted claims and dependencies from curated exploration, and Ansatze, a community platform for inspecting, guiding and checking this work. item.title: A Lean Formalization of the Hamilton--Perelman Proof of the Three-Dimensional Poincaré Conjecture
item.description: We formalize the smooth three-dimensional Poincaré conjecture, together with the Moise smoothing theorem, yielding the topological three-dimensional Poincaré conjecture. The smooth proof follows the Hamilton--Perelman route through Ricci flow with surgery and finite-time extinction. — Ziyang Qin, Yuan Liao, Ayush Khaitan, Bennett Chow — arXiv: lean / arXiv: ricci

item.title: Exact rational certificates and a Lean formalization of the eleven-variable Vasc inequality
item.description: We prove that the cyclic sum $\sum_{i=0}^{10}(x_i-x_{i+1})/(x_{i+1}+x_{i+2})$ is nonnegative for every strictly positive real eleven-tuple, with indices taken modulo eleven. item.title: Improving the lower bound on the Laughlin gap: An SDP search
item.description: A recent preprint by OpenAI resolved the spherical fermionic Laughlin spectral-gap conjecture for the full $V_1$ interaction by a Fock-space inequality: $H_Q^2\ge γH_Q$ on the lowest-Landau-level Fock space for all large flux $Q$ and every $γ$ below $0.0461673\ldots$, so that the gap above the Laughlin state at filling $1/3$ is at least $1/25$. item.title: NanoProof: Open and Efficient Automated Theorem Proving in Lean 4
item.description: We introduce NanoProof, to our knowledge the first factorized execution-guided theorem prover in Lean 4 whose training data, extraction tooling, training pipeline, and weights are all released, making it end-to-end reproducible using open-source resources. To this end, we build and release a dataset of structured proof trees, as well as a tool for programmatic interaction and data extraction within the Lean 4 formal verifier. item.title: Humanize Olympiad Agents: A Multi-Session Workflow for Olympiad Problem Solving with Solve, Review, Wiki, Verify
item.description: Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly improving on long-horizon scientific and olympiad tasks. Recent systems have produced a Lean-formalized resolution of the Navier--Stokes problem and autonomous solutions to four open questions in the Erdős Conjectures database. Yet neither system releases both its underlying model and complete inference stack. More broadly, a single agent session remains brittle on difficult problems: early errors can propagate, missing domain knowledge can stall progress, and… — Zhengyang Zhang, Jing Xiong, Hongzhou Lin, Juihui Chung, Zijian Zhang, Song Han — arXiv: lean / arXiv: navier

item.title: Cost-Efficient Theorem Proving via Agent Orchestration in Program Verification
item.description: Program verification establishes software correctness through machine-checkable proofs constructed in theorem provers. It's a guarantee especially valuable for code generated by large language models (LLMs), which is fluent but carries no assurance of correctness. item.title: Natural Language to First-Order Logic LLM-based Autoformalization
item.description: Large Language Models (LLMs) have renewed interest in autoformalization. Yet, when First-Order Logic (FOL) is considered as the target formalism, the field still lacks a unified task formulation and a systematic survey. item.title: SCOPE: Certified Theorem Proving with a Language Model as the Policy Planner
item.description: In proof assistants such as Lean, a generated proof must pass machine compilation checks, so evaluation needs no human scoring. Direct generation fails on multi-step numeric propositions: a proof is valid only if every content integer is correct, so the pass rate is bounded by the k-th power of the per-integer accuracy. Controlled corruption across 2,617 reference proofs confirms this power law. item.title: AIProver: Agentic Auto-Formalization of Mathematical Research via Certificate-Driven Evolving Harness
item.description: Proof auto-formalization translates natural-language (NL) theorems and proofs into a formal language (FL) such as Lean, enabling mechanical verification. Despite rapid progress, research-level proofs often depend on concepts missing from leading proof assistant libraries (e.g., Lean's Mathlib), and successful compilation does not guarantee that a translation preserves the theorem's meaning or the proof's reasoning. item.title: Toward a Lean Formalization of Analog Computing with Microwaves
item.description: Analog computing with microwave signals can perform linear transformations directly in the analog domain, as the signals propagate through a microwave network. A fundamental question is which transformations can be computed with a given set of microwave components. item.title: Borcea's 2-variance conjecture
item.description: In this paper, we prove Borcea's 2-variance conjecture. The Lean 4 formalization of the main results are also provided. — Teng Zhang — arXiv: lean

item.title: Predicting the Next State Is Not Enough: JEPA Representations for Lean Theorem Proving
item.description: Neural theorem provers must both propose tactics and decide which valid successor states to explore. item.title: When Does Structured Knowledge Help Neural Theorem Proving?
item.description: Does structured mathematical knowledge help LLMs prove theorems in Lean 4? If so, for which models, and does the answer vary by problem? Formal libraries such as Mathlib encode 285,000+ verified theorems with syntactic dependencies, but the semantic layer mathematicians rely on for discovery (analogies, generalizations, cross-domain bridges) remains implicit. item.title: Preserving Mathematical Reasoning in Compressed Diffusion Language Models via Trajectory-Aware Low-Rank Approximation
item.description: Diffusion language model (dLLM) compression faces a known challenge because calibration is typically performed on clean, fully visible activations, whereas inference traverses partially masked intermediate states. For low-rank compression, this raises two questions. item.title: Growing an Agent/Prover Interface: Evolutionary Tool Design for Cost-Efficient Theorem Proving in Rocq and Lean
item.description: Recent achievements in AI-assisted mathematics require intensive interaction of agents with proof assistants to generate machine-checked proof certificates. Agents interact with proof assistants such as Rocq or Lean through an interface that controls what the agent receives from the prover and the cost of these interactions. Today, these interfaces are adapted from tools designed for humans and not optimized for agents. item.title: Law And Order: Tax Law Autoformalization
item.description: Legal systems are increasingly implemented through software, yet scalable methods for translating legal texts into accurate symbolic representations remain underdeveloped. We study this problem through tax law, where forms and filing instructions define large computational structures involving arithmetic, branching, recursion, and tabular reasoning. We propose Law&Order, a neuro-symbolic framework for automatically formalizing tax forms and instructions into executable symbolic programs. Our approach establishes… — Sophia Simeng Han, Yoshiki Takashima, Anjiang Wei, Zhaoyu Li, Michael Genesereth — arXiv: autoformal

item.title: Machine-Checked Computational Group Theory in Lean 4: Operational Schreier-Sims Stabilizer Chains, BSGS Sifting, and Backtrack Ordered Partitions
item.description: We present gap-lean4-port (Release v0.2.0), a machine-checked formalization of foundational algorithms in computational discrete algebra and permutation group theory within the Lean 4 interactive theorem prover and Mathlib4.
